summary: The output of a design team analyzing different IPv6 link models for IEEE 802.16 networks. It examines considerations for each model and where each fits under different deployment scenarios. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Wi-Fi-like radio links are point-to-multipoint and connection-oriented, and they do not carry multicast both ways, so IPv6 does not fit them neatly. This memo compares three ways to paper over that: treat everyone as one shared link, give each device a link of its own, or make the network behave like an old Ethernet cable.

subtitle: Three ways to decide what counts as a link when IPv6 runs over a Wi-Fi-like radio network.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 is a point-to-multipoint, connection-oriented radio technology with no bi-directional multicast, so IPv6, which assumes a shared link with multicast, does not fit it neatly. There was no agreed answer to what should count as an IPv6 link over such a network.
tldr.mechanism: A design team compared three link models: one shared prefix for all stations, one unique prefix per station, and one that emulates an Ethernet broadcast link. For each it examined prefix assignment, address autoconfiguration, duplicate address detection, multicast support, packet forwarding and where the model fits in practice.
tldr.outcome: The conclusion is that the Ethernet-like model suits deployments using the Ethernet convergence sublayer, and the point-to-point model suits the IP convergence sublayer, with the shared prefix model left for the service provider community if it wants it. The document is informational and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem: What Counts as a Link
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 is a point-to-multipoint, connection-oriented access technology for the last mile, and it has no bi-directional native multicast support. Only downlink multicast is defined. That leaves two ways to run IP protocols that traditionally assume multicast is available at the link layer. One is to use bridging, such as IEEE 802.1D, to support bi-directional multicast. The other is to treat the MAC transport connections between a mobile station and a base station as point-to-point IP links, so that IP protocols such as ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery run without problems.

Commercial network models complicate this further. WiMAX defines a transport connection that extends the IEEE 802.16 MAC transport connection all the way to an access router, using a tunnel between the base station and the access router, and that leads to multiple ways of deploying IP over IEEE 802.16 networks. The document looks at the considerations in selecting a link model, analyses the possible models, and finally recommends one link model for a given deployment.

The vocabulary follows the IP over IEEE 802.16 problem statement, with additions. An access router is an entity that performs an IP routing function to provide IP connectivity for mobile stations; in WiMAX networks it is an Access Service Network Gateway. The Access Service Network is the complete set of network functions needed to provide radio access to a WiMAX subscriber, and it is the access network to which the station attaches; the IPv6 access router is one entity within it. Dormant mode is a state in which a mobile station restricts its ability to receive normal IP traffic by monitoring radio channels less often, which saves power and reduces signaling load; the station listens only at scheduled intervals on the paging channel, and the network keeps state about it so it can page it when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary IPv6 assumes every device on a link can hear every other one, which is what multicast is for. This radio technology does not work that way, so something has to be decided: is the link the whole radio network, or is it one base station and one device?

sections.title: The Shared IPv6 Prefix Model
sections.content:
In this model all mobile stations attached to an access router share one or more prefixes for building their global IPv6 addresses, and the prefixes advertised on the link are used by every station on it. The link between the station and the access router is viewed as a shared link at the IPv6 layer, while the lower layer link between the station and the base station is point-to-point, and that point-to-point link is extended all the way to the access router when the tunnel between base station and router is per station. An access router can serve one or more base stations, and all stations connected to base stations served by that router are on the same IPv6 link. Unlike the Ethernet-like model, this one gives the IPv6 layer no native link-layer multicast or broadcast.

The prefixes are advertised with the autonomous flag set and the on-link flag reset, so that nodes do not make an on-link assumption for addresses in those prefixes, and the standard IPv6 address autoconfiguration mechanisms are used. Duplicate address detection does not adapt well to the 802.16 air interface, because there is no native multicast. The RFC therefore proposes Relay DAD, in which the access router keeps the MLD table listing the multicast addresses and the nodes that joined them, and relays the duplicate address detection probe to the address owner when there is a conflict. The station builds a link-local address, constructs the corresponding solicited-node multicast address and sends an MLD Join request, starts checking uniqueness by sending a DAD neighbour solicitation on the initial MAC transport connection, and the router looks in the MLD table: if there is no entry it silently discards the probe, and if there is a match it relays it to the address owner. The owner defends the address with a DAD neighbour advertisement relayed back through the router, and the originating station assigns the address to its interface if it receives no response, or discards the tentative address if it does.

On reuse of existing specifications, the model needs no protocol changes but does require implementation changes for the duplicate address detection optimization on the router. There is no native on-link multicast, though a backend process in the router can keep the multicast member list and forward multicast packets to the members in a unicast manner, using MLD snooping to maintain that list. The definition of an IPv6 link is consistent for all procedures except native on-link multicast. All packets travel to the access router before being delivered, since the layer 2 transport connection is between the station and the router; the router normally handles packets with external IPv6 addresses, but packets with link-local destination addresses are relayed by the router without decrementing the hop limit. No host implementation change is needed, while the router needs MLD snooping for Relay DAD. The model suits shared on-link services together with the IP convergence sublayer with IPv6 classifiers, but in public access networks such as cellular networks it cannot be used for end users to share personal devices or services, and it was under consideration by the WiMAX Forum Network Working Group for IPv6 convergence sublayer access.
sections.plainLanguage: The first model treats the radio network as one big shared link: every device gets its address from the same prefix. The catch is that checking for duplicate addresses normally needs multicast, which this radio technology does not have, so the router has to keep a list of who joined which group and pass the check messages along itself.

sections.title: The Point-to-Point Model
sections.content:
In this model the set of MAC transport connections between a station and the access router is treated as a single link, following the recommendations of the third-generation partnership project document. Each link between a station and the router is allocated its own unique prefix, or set of unique prefixes, by the router, and no other node under that router has the same prefixes on its link. There are three ways to implement the point-to-point link. One is to run PPP on the link, which requires the IEEE 802.16 link to use the Ethernet convergence sublayer and PPP over Ethernet, so whether PPP can be run depends on the network architecture. Another is, where the physical medium is shared like Ethernet but PPP is not run, to make the link point-to-point by putting each station on a separate VLAN. The third is, if neither PPP nor VLAN is used, to view the set of IEEE 802.16 connections as a virtual point-to-point link.

Prefixes are assigned using the standard Router Advertisement mechanism, with the router allocating a unique prefix or set of unique prefixes for each station, and both the autonomous flag and the on-link flag set to 1 because the prefixes can be used for autoconfiguration and are on the link. Stations perform link-local and global address autoconfiguration exactly as specified, including duplicate address detection. Because there is only one other node on the link, the router, the only possible conflict is with the router itself, so collisions are statistically very unlikely and easy to fix. If DHCP is used, the server must provide addresses with a separate prefix per station, matching a prefix the router has advertised.

The solution reuses the existing Neighbor Discovery and address autoconfiguration specifications and, if PPP is used, the PPP-over-IPv6 and PPP-over-Ethernet specifications, with no protocol changes required, only proper configuration; without PPP, any VLAN solution such as IEEE 802.1Q or any layer 2 tunnel can be used. Because the link is point-to-point, any multicast can only be sent by one node or the other, and link-local multicast between other nodes and the router is not seen. The IP link is fully consistent with a standard point-to-point link, without exception. The station always sends all packets to the router, since it is the only other node on the link, and link-local unicast and multicast packets are forwarded only between the two. Host implementations follow standard IPv6 stack procedures with no changes. If PPP is used, no router changes are needed; otherwise the router must give each station a separate VLAN or an layer 2 tunnel that aggregates the connections and presents them as one interface to the IPv6 layer, and must be configured with a unique prefix or set of prefixes per station, included in every Router Advertisement, with DHCP leases limited to those prefixes. The model suits deployments with no shared services in the access network, such as service provider networks like cellular networks that give the public access to wireless networks. It is not appropriate for enterprise networks, where shared services such as printers and fax machines are discovered using a link-local service discovery protocol, because it makes no shared link services possible in the access network.
sections.plainLanguage: The second model gives every device a link of its own, with its own address prefix. It is the simplest for the duplicate address check, because there is only one other node to collide with, and it needs no new protocol. What it cannot do is let devices on the same base station see each other, which rules it out where people share printers.

sections.title: The Ethernet-Like Model
sections.content:
The third model configures and provisions an IEEE 802.16 network so that it emulates a broadcast link in a manner similar to Ethernet, and it works as the Neighbor Discovery and address autoconfiguration specifications describe. One way to construct such a link is to implement bridging between the base stations and the access router, like a switched Ethernet, where the bridging performs link aggregation between the base stations and the router and also supports multicast packet filtering.

Prefixes are assigned as specified, address autoconfiguration is the same as in the standard specification, and duplicate address detection is the same too. All the IPv6 standards can be preserved or reused in this model. On-link multicast can be emulated in a unicast manner by efficiently bridging between all the base stations, with IEEE 802.16 providing the links between the stations and the bridge on top of the base station, and MLD snooping should be used for efficient forwarding of multicast packets. Nevertheless, in the case of bridging, direct communication between stations may not be allowed because of service provider restrictions. The model is consistent with the IP link definition, and when properly configured and assisted by simple bridging, IEEE 802.16 can emulate a simple broadcast network like Ethernet. There is no special impact on host implementation. There is also no special impact on router implementation under a separated base-station-to-router model if the bridging is implemented in the base station, though some networks such as WiMAX may require bridging to be implemented in the access router. The model works with the Ethernet convergence sublayer, and it is the one chosen for fixed and nomadic WiMAX networks by the WiMAX Forum Network Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The third model makes the radio network behave like an old shared Ethernet cable: stations can see each other, multicast works, and the standard IPv6 rules apply unchanged. It needs bridging between the base stations, which is the usual way to build a switched network.

sections.title: Renumbering, Dormant Mode and Routing
sections.content:
Renumbering. If the downstream prefixes managed by the router are involved in renumbering, it may be necessary to renumber each link under that router. If the prefixes are advertised in Router Advertisements, the router must withdraw the existing prefixes and advertise new ones. Because each station, whatever the link model, is on a separate point-to-point link at the MAC level, the router must send a Router Advertisement withdrawing the old prefix and advertising the new one to each link. In the point-to-point model the number of advertisements sent equals the number of nodes the router serves, whereas in the other two models the router sends a single advertisement to the base station, which is sent to all the stations as separate advertisements. If DHCP assigns the addresses, either the lease lifetime may be reduced before the renumbering to encourage stations to renew quickly, or a DHCP Reconfigure message may be sent to each station by the server to cause it to renew. The amount of traffic on the air interface is the same for all link models, but the number of advertisements sent by the router to the base station can be compared between the models.

Dormant mode. When the network needs to deliver packets to a station in dormant mode, the router pages it, the station receives the page on the paging channel and transitions to active mode, requests and obtains the radio resources, and the network can then deliver the packets; in many networks packets for a dormant station are buffered at the router until connectivity is established. Support for dormant stations is critical in mobile networks, so it is a necessary feature, and paging capability and the optimizations possible for paging are neither enhanced nor handicapped by the link model itself. However, multicast capability within a link may cause a station to wake up for an unwanted packet, which can be avoided by filtering the multicast packets and delivering them only to the stations listening for them. Since the shared prefix model has no multicast capability and the point-to-point model has only one node on the link, neither affects dormant mode. The Ethernet-like model may have multicast capability, which requires filtering at the base station.

Routing. The model used in an IEEE 802.16 network may have a significant impact on how routing protocols are run over it. The deployment model presented in the document is the least impacting one on routing, because connectivity on the provider edge is intentionally limited to point-to-point connectivity from one base station to any one of multiple stations. Any other deployment model may cause a significant impact on routing protocols, though those are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Three practical effects. Renumbering means sending new addresses to every station, and the point-to-point model needs one message per station. A dormant station has to be woken with a page, and only the Ethernet-like model can wake it for a multicast it did not want. And the link model can shape how routing protocols run over the network, which is why the document favours the point-to-point case.

sections.title: Conclusions and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The conclusion is that Ethernet-like link models are used when the deployment requires the Ethernet convergence sublayer, since it is the only model proposed for that sublayer and running IPv6 over Ethernet is well understood. For the IP convergence sublayer with IPv6 classifiers, a point-to-point link model appears to be the choice, because of its simplicity for performing duplicate address detection, because it does not break any existing applications, and because it requires no new protocol to be defined. The IPv6 shared prefix model would be defined if there is any interest from the service provider community.

The security considerations state that the document is an analysis of link models and so introduces no new security threats, and that whatever the link model, the networks employ the same link-layer security mechanisms defined in IEEE 802.16e. The chosen link model does affect the scope of link-local communication, and that has security implications for protocols designed to work within the link scope: this is the concern for a shared link model, where private resources such as a personal printer cannot be put onto a public WiMAX network, which may restrict the usage of a shared prefix model to enterprise environments. The Neighbor Discovery related security issues are documented elsewhere and apply to all the models described. Model specific security considerations are documented in their respective protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendation is to pick the model that matches the kind of network you have: the Ethernet-like one where the Ethernet layer is used, and the point-to-point one everywhere else, because it is simplest and breaks nothing. The one thing to watch is how much of your network is link-local and therefore visible to others.
